newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris air cargo market sees little prospect of rates increases in the Autumn.
newsitem.headline: Paris air cargo market sees little prospect of rates increases in the Autumn.

text.p: The Paris air cargo market sees little prospect of rates increases in the Autumn but it is still hopeful of a strong final quarter to what has been a mediocre year, a Reuters report showed.
Stagnant economic output in France in 1996 is reflected in the level of export traffic handled at the country's main gateways, Charles de Gaulle and Orly.
The latest available figures from the airport authority showed that ex-Paris freight volumes for the period January-July 1996, totalled 335,486 tonnes, down 2.2 percent on 1995 levels.

"Government forecasts for French GDP growth in 1996 of 2.4 percent have proved to be well-short of the mark, this being currently more in the order of 1.2 percent. Growth in the final quarter of the year will certainly be superior to that of the two previous quarters but not as good as September-December 1995," said Klaus Pfab, the chairman of France's air freight forwarding agents association, SNAGFA.
Pfab said it is difficult to see any guiding principle in the cargo rates' policies of the airlines. Given the current economic climate, it would be timely for rates to stay as they are, he added.
The vast majority of ex-Paris rates stayed firm during the summer season and feedback from airlines and forwarders is that the status quo looks set to prevail into the foreseeable future.

"While we don't see rates going up, at the same time, there are no noticeable downward pressures. It's a relatively stable period," said Adrien Thominet, of French general sales agent,Aero Cargo International.
One minor exception is the Paris-Dubai market, where extra ex-Paris capacity in recent months has seen average rates fall by around 20 centimes/kilo since July 1996, sources said.

Another example of a slight erosion in rates is the Paris-Johannesburg route - a result of South African Airways SAA.CN imposing reductions of around six percent since July 1996 in order to fall more into line with the average market rate, a spokesman for the airline said.

On prime Far East routes from Paris, notably to Tokyo, Seoul and Hong Kong, increased capacity and strong competition from off-line carriers has continued to create an abundance of capacity making the prospect of increases slim, said market insiders.

"Market conditions are just not right for increases. We are still very much in a stagnant phase and capacity is readily available between Paris and Tokyo," a Japan Airlines (JAL), cargo official told Reuters
For All Nippon Airlines (ANA), the next fortnight should reveal what lies ahead in terms of market demand in the final quarter of the year.

"What's clear is that the current period is not as strong as last year. An increase in rates is improbable and while there are no immediate pressures on rates, we'll be content to keep them stable," an ANA cargo official said."

Korean Airlines (KAL) recently said it intended to increase ex-Europe rates by five to ten percent during the Autumn to Seoul and Japan, although an exact date for their implementation had not yet been decided on.
KAL's Paris cargo manager, Christian Prochasson, said if KAL did increase its ex-Paris rates it would probably be by around five percent.

"Demand is not that strong at present but at least one encouraging sign in the first eight months of the year was that our ex-Paris tonnage rose by four percent on 1995 levels. We are stil hopeful of a strong finish to the year."
As far as Paris-U.S. routes are concerned, the summer months produced a buoyant level of spot-rating activity - a sure indication of low volumes and abundant capacity, said one industry source.
One insider told Reuters that the French government's policy of maintaining a strong franc against the U.S. dollar had had the effect of keeping export volumes static and rates under pressure.

"By contrast,the UK market,for example,is more bullish as a result of a constant exchange rate between sterling and the dollar and this has provided some scope, albeit limited perhaps, for rate increases. The fact there's little sign of relaxation in this monetary policy means the Paris-U.S market will continue to be depressed," he commented.
Several Paris-based U.S. carriers told Reuters they had no plans to increase in the Autumn.
"We don't expect any increases in our our rates before the end of the year, it being hard enough to maintain them at their current level," a Continental Airlines, cargo official said.

Another major U.S. carrier echoed this point of view. "We're doing our upmost to keep rates steady and to date have managed to do so. We expect some relief in the Autumn when, traditionally, the market strengthens and capacity is tighter."
One bright note in the past week or so, has been an increase in the number of telephone requests for spot quotations, he said. "However, it's unlikely we'll reach the level of the summer months."
More than one transatlantic carrier complained of the negative impact on volumes of stricter security measures at the Paris airports in the wake of the TWA crash in July.
These stipulate that freight must remain in airlines' warehouses for 24 hours after deposit, while all urgent shipments are subjected to X-ray screening or inspection by sniffer dogs.

"It's difficult to say how much business has been drained away from Paris by off-line carriers operating on U.S. routes because of transit delays. We'll have a better idea as the current month progresses."
